summary: angle of twist (ϕ) is what the Torsional stiffness calculator works out, and it gets there from the internal torque, the torsional stiffness (k), the polar moment of inertia and the beam length. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Torsional stiffness calculator work?
sections.html:
The Torsional stiffness calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports angle of twist (ϕ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the material (optional)); then you type in the internal torque (T), the torsional stiffness (k) (k = T/ϕ), the polar moment of inertia (J) and the beam length (L).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in newton meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 18 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in newton meters per radian. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 10 options, such as aluminum — 2014-T6 alloy, aluminum — 6061-T6 alloy and cast iron — Gray ASTM 20 alloy. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in quartic meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 5 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Torsional stiffness calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Angle of twist (ϕ)=internal torque (T) ÷ torsional stiffness (k)
Torsional stiffness (k)=polar moment of inertia (J) × shear modulus (G) ÷ beam length (L)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in radians, and convertible to any of the 12 units on that chip.
  • Shown in newton meters per radian, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in gigapascals, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Torque, opening in newton meters
  • Angle, opening in radians
  • Torque per angle, opening in newton meters per radian
  • Pressure, opening in gigapascals
  • Second moment of area, opening in quartic meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Torque per angle, opening in newton meters per radian

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Torsional stiffness calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the internal torque, the torsional stiffness (k) and the polar moment of inertia — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Torsional stiffness calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns angle of twist (ϕ), derived from the internal torque, the torsional stiffness (k) and the polar moment of inertia. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Torsional stiffness calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the internal torque, the torsional stiffness (k), the polar moment of inertia and the beam length, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter internal torque (T) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Internal torque (T) opens in newton meters and the chip beside it offers 18 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Shear modulus (G) = 0 GPa. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Torsional stiffness calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
